description:
We are Shahar and Shay, a married couple bringing together two very different but complementary worlds: space engineering and data engineering.

Shay is a space researcher with a PhD in Mechanical Engineering. He works on space-related research and is the inventor of StarHab, a concept focused on future space habitats. He brings strong expertise in space systems, engineering, and the practical challenges of operating in extreme environments.

I’m Shahar, a Data Platform Engineer specializing in data engineering and cybersecurity. I enjoy turning complex datasets and problems into intuitive, useful tools. Outside of tech, I’m a BJJ blue belt — so I’m also used to solving problems under pressure and adapting quickly. :)

We chose the CLPS Lunar Mission Browser challenge because it sits exactly at the intersection of our skills: space exploration, engineering, data, and software. We’re excited to build something that can turn complex mission data into an intuitive experience for people who need to make decisions about lunar landing sites and mission conditions.
summary: Moonat is a web app that shows the Moon's sky from any point on its surface, at any time. It works like a map app for the Moon: click places on a 3D globe or search for missions such as Apollo 11, pick dates (it suggests the best ones for sunlight, Earth contact or a visible eclipse), and plan rover trips with stops. Moonat places the Sun and Earth with JPL ephemerides, checks whether a ridge or crater rim hides them using NASA LOLA terrain (fetched live from Moon Trek for any point), and reports the sunlight and Earth contact a lander, rover or base would get, including eclipses of the Sun by the Earth. A first-person sky view shows it all, and the map shows where each view is looking and where it is day or night at that moment. Map layers show NASA's permanently shadowed regions and most sunlit ground at the poles, and many sites and dates compare side by side. In AI mode, a user describes a mission in plain words; Claude turns it into requirements and uses Moonat's validated physics as tools to suggest and rank sites and dates. We used Moonat to choose a site for a lunar base: the Malapert massif crest, which over 2030-2040 gets 82% of full sunlight on average and keeps 98% of the Earth's disk in view on average (the Earth never fully sets there).
details:
WHAT IT DOES

  • Inputs, in the order a user thinks (like a map app): places, chosen by clicking the 3D Moon globe (near side, far side or either pole), by dropping and dragging a pin, or by searching "Search the Moon" (missions from Apollo to Beresheet, each marked with the flag of the nation that flew it, potential Artemis sites, polar ridges, or coordinates). A Layers button adds base maps (imagery, elevation colours), contour lines, and NASA's permanently shadowed regions and most sunlit ground. Several places compare side by side. Each has a start time and an end time or a duration, picked from a calendar that suggests the best dates for that place. Advanced: a rover trip from the place to an end point, with any number of stops, and a rover type as the "travel mode".
  • Sun data: elevation, azimuth, how much of the solar disk clears the terrain and the Earth, solar flux (W/m2) on a Sun-facing panel, on a panel turning on a vertical mast at a fixed tilt, or on flat ground, time to sunset, eclipses.
  • Earth data: elevation, azimuth, how much of the Earth is visible (a proxy for direct radio contact), its phase, time to Earthset. A Sun | Earth | Both switch shows either or both on the same charts.
  • Sky view: a first-person 3D view from 2 m above the ground that fills the window like an app, with a wedge on the map showing where it looks: real terrain lit by the Sun, the Earth with its true phase and orientation, stars and planets. During an eclipse the Earth covers the Sun and its atmosphere glows as a red ring (an illustrative drawing; the geometry and timing are computed).
  • Suggested dates: the best windows for solar power, for direct-to-Earth contact and for both, every eclipse of the Sun by the Earth visible from the place, and Earthrises at polar and limb sites.
  • Rover trips: the fastest route through all stops within the rover's slope limit, drawn on the globe, with elevation and slope profiles and the Sun and Earth along the drive. The travel time is coloured like traffic in a map app, by how much slower the route is than a straight drive on flat ground. Pressing play drives the route in the sky view, optionally in a driver's view.
  • Map: day and night at the chosen moment, including the Earth's shadow during eclipses.
  • AI mode: describe a mission in plain words. The AI states its assumptions as requirements, screens candidate sites, evaluates the best ones with Moonat's own physics and real terrain, suggests dates, and ranks the sites with the computed numbers. One click puts them on the map.
  • Mission durations from hours to years become timelines, one line per scenario. Playback can follow the Sun or the Earth. Every view can be shared as a link. It works on phones.

HOW IT WORKS AND HOW WE VALIDATED IT

  1. Positions: JPL DE421 ephemeris and the lunar orientation model (MOON_ME frame, with libration), with light-time and aberration. Against JPL Horizons, the Sun and Earth directions agree to 0.055 arcseconds at worst (399 comparisons).
  2. Terrain: NASA LRO LOLA elevation maps give the horizon in every direction, out to 70-330 km, including lunar curvature. Checked against published south-pole illumination (Glaser et al. 2014): 92.7% lit vs 92.5% published. Checked against real Apollo photos: the skyline in NASA photos AS15-88-11863 (Hadley Delta), AS15-86-11603 (Mount Hadley) and AS16-113-18339 (Stone Mountain) matches our horizon to 0.08-0.15 degrees RMS, and the Sun's altitude at 43 Apollo times in the Apollo Lunar Surface Journal matches to 0.016 degrees RMS.
  3. Visibility: the share of the Sun's or Earth's disk above that skyline, weighted for limb darkening for power.
  4. The browser reproduces our Python reference to 3e-11 degrees; an independent check of the browser code against JPL Horizons at 20 random places and times agrees to 0.13 arcseconds.
  5. Terrain anywhere: for any other point, the browser fetches LOLA heights from NASA Moon Trek in 1-3 s and traces the horizon itself (0.07-0.37 degrees RMS against our precomputed horizons at 10 of 12 test sites).
  6. Eclipses: NASA's contact times of the lunar eclipses of 14 March 2025 (seen by Blue Ghost) and 24 April 1967 (seen by Surveyor 3) are reproduced to 4.2 s or better.
  7. Rover trips: a shortest-time path search through every stop on a Moon Trek elevation grid, with VIPER-class (0.2 m/s, 15 degrees) and Apollo LRV (2.5 m/s, 20 degrees) presets from NASA sources.
  8. Suggested dates: a two-year scan of sunlight, Earth visibility and eclipses in a background thread; it finds every umbral lunar eclipse in NASA's 2025-2030 catalog.
  9. Base siting: 80,648 south-polar points screened and the best refined at 20 m resolution over 2030-2040; the recommended site (Malapert massif crest) matches Glaser et al. within 0.2 points and NASA's Earth-visibility map with r = 0.97.
  10. AI mode: Claude (Anthropic) never computes physics itself; it calls tools that run Moonat's validated code, and the result cards show the tools' numbers.

TOOLS: Python (skyfield, numpy), JavaScript (three.js, Plotly), GitHub Pages.

WHY IT MATTERS: The challenge asks for rapid, intuitive comparison of landing sites and dates near the south pole. We built that, and generalised it to the whole Moon and to rover trips. At the poles a few hundred metres or a few days decide whether a lander has power and contact with Earth; Moonat makes that visible in seconds, for anyone from a child to a mission planner.
